title: Implicit Differentiation: Slope Along a Level Curve
topic: A curve defined implicitly by f(x, y) = c has slope dy/dx = -f_x / f_y. Because f stays constant along the curve, its total differential vanishes: f_x dx + f_y dy = 0. Geometrically the tangent is perpendicular to the gradient, so the slope is read straight off the partial derivatives. Demonstrated on the tilted ellipse x^2 + xy + y^2 = 2 by sliding a point around it and tracking the live slope.

beats.narration: Some curves twist so much you can never solve for y. Can we still find their slope?

elements.content: A curve you can't solve — what's its slope?

beats.narration: Here is a curve where f of x and y stays equal to a constant. The gradient of f points straight across it, at a right angle everywhere.

elements.content: Tilted ellipse f(x,y)=2 in amber, axes in chalk-200
Gradient arrow at one sample point, perpendicular to the curve, rose
f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² = c
∇f crosses the curve at a right angle.

beats.narration: Walk a tiny step along the curve and f does not change. So f sub x times d x plus f sub y times d y is zero, which rearranges to d y by d x equals minus f sub x over f sub y.

elements.content: No need to solve for y — just take partials.

beats.narration: Slide the point around the curve. At every spot the tangent slope is exactly minus f sub x over f sub y, and it turns as the gradient turns.

elements.content: Ellipse held lit; a point P slides around it
Tangent line at P (perpendicular to gradient) rotating as P moves
Gradient arrow ∇f at P, perpendicular to tangent
Live readout: dy/dx = −f_x/f_y updates with P

beats.narration: Constant along the curve means the change cancels — so the slope is minus the x partial over the y partial.

elements.content: 'The slope is just minus f_x over f_y.' serif italic
